newsitem.title: CHILE: U.S. to have fast-track trade law by March - Daley.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to have fast-track trade law by March - Daley.

text.p: The Clinton adminstration expects to have "fast-track" authority for its negotiators by the time Western Hemisphere free trade talks begin in March 1998, U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley said on Monday.
Daley, in Chile for a three-day visit, said the White House was still testing the political waters to decide when to push for a vote in Congress on fast-track legislation.
"We're in consultations with people in Congress ... to find a way to move this forward and have it, hopefully, obviously, in time for Santiago next March," Daley told a news conference.

The leaders of every country in the Americas except Cuba will meet in the Chilean capital in March for a follow-up to a 1994 Miami summit at which they will begin formal talks on establishing a Free Trade Area of the Americas.
Fast track would also clear the way for the North American Free Trade Area to expand by including Chile and later other countries.

Chile, with the region's most prosperous economy, has been nagging the United States to deliver on a long-standing invitation to it to join NAFTA, the free-trade agreement that joins the United States, Canada and Mexico.
Chile has said it will not begin trade talks with the United States unless the American negotiators have fast-track authority approved by Congress.

If they have such authority, Congress will only be able to vote yes or no on a finished treaty, not propose amendments. Without it, Chileans fear a treaty expanding NAFTA will be picked apart by special-interest groups in Congress.
Daley said he reassured the Chileans that President Bill Clinton was committed to getting fast track passed -- when he had the votes.

"The commitment of the president is very strong for fast track. Quite honestly, we have been disappointed that we have not been able to find the right time, politically speaking, to move that piece of legislation forward," he said.
"Our goal is to have a successful fight, not just to have a fight," he said. "We're trying to gauge now what would be the right time for a successful fight."
Fast-track legislation has been deadlocked in Congress over the Republican majority's refusal to allow labor and environmental standards to be included in the agenda of future trade talks.

Asked about news reports saying Cuba would like to participate in the March summit, Daley said he could understand Cuba's interest in participating but it remained the only non-elected government in the Western Hemisphere.
"I don't blame Cuba for wanting to be involved, but it's really a statement that there is only one country left where people are not free to express themselves," he said.
Daley, who arrived from Argentina on Saturday night, was due to meet President Eduardo Frei and Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat later on Monday and return to Washington on Tuesday.
